description_full: Ethan Allen Interiors Inc. operates as an interior design company, and manufacturer and retailer of home furnishings in the United States and internationally. The company operates through two segments: Wholesale and Retail. It offers case goods items, such as beds, dressers, armoires, tables, chairs, buffets, entertainment units, home office furniture, and wooden accents; upholstery comprising fabric-covered items, such as sleepers, recliners and other motion furniture, chairs, ottomans, custom pillows, sofas, loveseats, cut fabrics, and leather; and window treatments and drapery hardware, wall decors, florals, lighting, clocks, mattresses, bedspreads, throws, pillows, decorative accents, area rugs, flooring, wall coverings, and outdoor furnishings. The company also sells third-party furniture protection plans and sales less prompt payment discounts, sales allowances and other incentives. It markets and sells its products under the Ethan Allen brand through design centers, independent retailers, and other third parties as well as through ethanallen.com website. Ethan Allen Interiors Inc. was founded in 1932 and is headquartered in Danbury, Connecticut.

financial_summary: Ethan Allen Interiors Inc. is a small-cap consumer cyclical business with a $506M market cap on $579M of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at -10% over the past three years and -3% annually across the full decade, and a shrinking top line is the hardest headwind any business can overcome.

Returns on capital run at 16% against a 9% cost of capital, a 7-point spread that creates value, though narrow enough that competitive pressure could close it. Gross margins of 55% confirm genuine pricing power.

The business throws off $41M in free cash flow — roughly 7 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 1.32× so those profits are backed by real cash.
On the balance sheet, the balance sheet carries net cash, which is the gold standard: the business never has to make desperate decisions in a bad year.

Management returns a meaningful 10.1% of market cap to owners through dividends and buybacks, a strong signal of disciplined capital allocation, and insiders hold 13% of the shares, so management thinks like owners because it is one — the strongest alignment there is.

sect: Its 8% operating margin is roughly in line with the Consumer Cyclical median (8%).
It earns less of the sector's profit than its revenue share would suggest (0.94x).
Over five years it has been losing share of the sector profit pool (-7.7% a year).
The sector is fragmented and competitive (HHI 0.03 across 377 companies in the universe; the top four hold 26% of revenue), so pricing power is hard to come by.
mkt: The shares have drifted higher, up 10% over the past year excluding the latest month.
The price sits mid-way through its 52-week range, 21% below the high.
With annualised volatility of 29% and a beta of 0.82, it moves roughly with the market, though its beta has shifted (1y 0.01 vs 5y 0.78), so read it loosely.
About $10.6M trades a day, enough to build a position.
In past sell-offs it fell 53% in the 2020 crash, 26% in the 2022 bear market and 77% in 2008.
val: The stock trades 31% below its DCF fair value of $29.13, a meaningful margin of safety.
The fair-value models corroborate one another (dispersion 9%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $24.68 to $35.30 (P10-P90).
On multiples it looks cheap against Consumer Cyclical peers: P/E 12.9 vs 19.3, EV/EBITDA 8.3 vs 11.2 and P/FCF 12.2 vs 16.5 (sector median).
Against its own history it is dear: the EBIT multiple sits 104% above its 10-year median.
Earnings yields are attractive: an FCF yield of 8.2% (above the risk-free rate) and an EBIT/EV of 8.8% (vs the 8% bar).
The Street target $22.00 on average, 10% above the price.
prof: ROIC of 16% clears the cost of capital of 8.9% by 7pp, the mark of a value creator; returns have swung a lot from year to year (CV 0.60).
It runs a 55% gross margin and converts 7% of revenue into free cash flow.
Earnings quality looks solid: cash conversion of 1.32x.
ROE of 8% comes mostly from margins and asset turnover rather than leverage (1.5x equity multiplier).
It spends 0.2% of revenue on stock compensation.
hlth: The balance sheet carries net cash of $12.6M.
No distress or manipulation flags (Altman Z 4.0, in the safe zone).
Its debt comes due soon (maturity wall about 1.5 years out), so refinancing terms matter.
growth: Revenue has compounded at -9.9% over 3 years, -3.3% over 5 years and -3.1% over 10 years, so the decline is deepening.
Net reinvestment is nil (capex and working capital no more than cover depreciation), so fundamental growth is near zero.
Free cash flow has compounded -18.9% a year over five years, short of the 5% durability bar.
Capex runs only 0.7x depreciation (1.9% of sales), so the asset base is being harvested rather than grown.
Its Rule of 40 score is 4, below the 40 that marks a healthy growth business.
own: Insiders own 13.1%, meaningful skin in the game, and institutions hold 88%.
Insiders have only sold over the past year (20 sales, net $1.1M sold).
It returns 10.1% a year to shareholders (0.9% in buybacks and 7.8% in dividends).
It has paid a dividend for 29 consecutive years, raising it 1.3% a year over the last five.
Short interest is elevated at 12.1% of the float, 5.7 days to cover.
people: With about 3,062 employees, each generates about $189K of revenue, 0.5x the Consumer Cyclical median.
That works out to $14K of free cash flow per employee.
CEO pay is $1.7M (9x revenue per employee), and compensation governance scores well (2/10, lower is better).
